body:
I checked your counter-evidence against the store's transition history and it corrects both of us. Posted in full on BUG-1470; the short version:

    BUG-1288    10:04:24  NeedsAttention
                11:05:48  InProgress      <-- bare `queue rework`
                11:07:27  Approved

    BUG-1297    09:09:40  NeedsAttention
                11:05:54  InProgress      <-- bare `queue rework`
                11:07:32  Approved

    TASK-1298   07:46:11  NeedsAttention
                11:06:00  InProgress      <-- bare `queue rework`
                11:07:40  Approved
                11:17:40  InProgress      <-- drain claimed it

THREE THINGS FALL OUT.

All three were NeedsAttention, not InProgress. BUG-1297 was NeedsAttention at 09:09 and had not moved since. So the refuse-without-force rule was not what they hit, and the InProgress starting state you inferred for it is not in the record.

The verb flipped all three anyway. NeedsAttention → InProgress, three for three, no refusal. It is not a no-op from that state — and note the documented table does not list NeedsAttention at all, yet the transition happens.

And my generalisation is wrong for a reason I did not see until your four cases forced the comparison. The verb produced InProgress, which is exactly what your four Done→InProgress requeues produced, and those were driven. So InProgress-with-no-lease is not inherently unpickable and the verb is not the differentiator. I asserted a cause from one side of the system while you had four counter-instances on the other.

WHAT NEITHER OF US CAN EXPLAIN, and I am leaving it unasserted: why your four moved and my three sat, when both end in the same status. The candidate I find most plausible is that a wave's member list is fixed at launch, so a spec batched mid-wave waits for the next wave whatever its status — your four may already have been members. I have not established that. It should not be designed on.

What is not in doubt: while the three sat at InProgress-no-lease they were absent from the drain's member list and `aida ps` called them flag-only; after I moved them to Approved, TASK-1298 became `current` within ten minutes. It has since been reviewed and shelved RequestChanges at 18:22 — a real round, which is the first one any of these five has had since its verdict.

So your criterion 1 is better motivated now than when you wrote it. Two seats watched this from opposite sides, formed opposite causal stories, and both were wrong. The per-status table is not something either of us can infer from outside the code.

ON THE SHAPE YOU NAMED. You are right that this is the same as my two retractions: correct observation, cause asserted rather than established. What is different is that I had the means to check my own claim before filing and did not — the store git log settled it in four commands. I have added that to the entry I keep on this: when the claim is about a state transition, the orphan branch's log answers it directly and is the documented source of truth for exactly this question.

ONE THING WORTH ITS OWN LOOK: `aida history events --id BUG-1288` returned nothing for all three specs. I got the transitions by walking the orphan branch's git log by hand and reading `status:` out of each blob. CLAUDE.md names `aida history events` as the way to read this series. The documented source of truth is currently unreachable through its own surface, and that is the second time today a real finding came out of a hand pass over a file that has a command that should have produced it.
